passages.happening:
Isaiah sings a song. ‘I will sing for my beloved a song of his vineyard: My beloved had a vineyard on a very fertile hill’ (verse 1). He dug it up, cleared the stones, planted the finest vines, built a watchtower and cut a winepress. He waited for good grapes, but the fruit was sour (verse 2).

Then the owner speaks. He asks the people of Jerusalem and Judah to judge between him and his vineyard. ‘What more could I have done for My vineyard than I already did for it?’ (verse 4). Why did it give sour fruit? So he will take away its hedge and tear down its wall, let it be trampled and overgrown, and command the clouds not to rain on it (verses 5-6).

Then the meaning. ‘For the vineyard of the LORD of Hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah are the plant of His delight. He looked for justice, but saw bloodshed; for righteousness, but heard a cry of distress’ (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
Vineyards were a major investment in Israel's hill country. A farmer had to clear the rocky soil, terrace the slope, plant choice vines, build a stone watchtower to guard the harvest and cut a winepress into the bedrock. It took years before the vines produced. A vineyard that gave sour, wild grapes after all that labor was a disaster.

The song begins like a love song, since vineyards were a common picture in love poetry. It draws the hearers in and asks them to judge the case before revealing that they are the accused, much as Nathan did with David.

The climax rests on two Hebrew wordplays that English cannot reproduce. God looked for mishpat, justice, and saw mispach, bloodshed. He looked for tsedaqah, righteousness, and heard tse'aqah, a cry of distress. The words sound almost the same and mean opposites. The fruit God wanted was not religious performance but justice and righteousness.
passages.later: A psalm tells the same story of God's care: ‘You uprooted a vine from Egypt; You drove out the nations and transplanted it’ (Psalm 80:8). Isaiah later sings a second vineyard song: ‘I, the LORD, am its keeper; I water it continually’ (Isaiah 27:3). And Jesus began a parable with this song's own details: ‘A man planted a vineyard. He put a wall around it, dug a wine vat, and built a watchtower’ (Mark 12:1).
passages.hard:
Is God harsh to destroy the vineyard he planted?

The song expects the objection. It puts the hearers in the judge's seat (verse 3) and asks what more the owner could have done (verse 4). Several things soften a reader's first impression. The judgment is described mostly as God withdrawing his care rather than attacking: the hedge removed, the wall broken, the rain held back. The fruit he wanted was justice for the vulnerable. And this is not the end of the vineyard. In chapter 27 Isaiah sings a second vineyard song, in which God guards and waters his vineyard and Israel fills the world with fruit.

This is Israel's own Scripture, a prophet's word to his own people about their own sin. It is not a reason to blame the Jewish people, then or now.
passages.asks: God looked for justice and found bloodshed, for righteousness and heard a cry. Ask what fruit God would find if he looked at your life this year. And ask whose cry of distress you might be the cause of.

passages.t: Woe to those who join house to house
passages.happening:
‘Woe to you who add house to house and join field to field until no place is left and you live alone in the land’ (verse 8). The LORD of Hosts has sworn that many great houses will stand empty (verse 9). Ten acres of vineyard will give only a bath of wine, and a homer of seed only an ephah of grain (verse 10).

‘Woe to those who rise early in the morning in pursuit of strong drink’ (verse 11). At their feasts there are lyres, harps, tambourines, flutes and wine. ‘They disregard the actions of the LORD and fail to see the work of His hands’ (verse 12).

‘Therefore My people will go into exile for their lack of understanding’ (verse 13). Sheol opens its jaws, and down go the nobles and revelers (verse 14). Mankind will be humbled, ‘But the LORD of Hosts will be exalted by His justice, and the holy God will show Himself holy in righteousness’ (verse 16). Lambs will graze among the ruins of the wealthy (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
Woe, hoy in Hebrew, is a cry used in mourning for the dead. When a prophet pronounces woe on the living, he is announcing a funeral in advance. Six woes follow the song, showing what the sour grapes look like in daily life.

The first is land-grabbing. In the prosperity of eighth-century Judah, wealth gathered into fewer hands. Israel's law meant land to stay with families as an inheritance from God, and the Jubilee law returned land to its families every fifty years, though there is little evidence it was regularly kept. The rich were buying out their neighbors until they lived alone in the land.

The curse of verse 10 is the reverse of a harvest. Ten acres would give about six gallons of wine, and the grain harvested would be a tenth of what was sown. Sheol is the realm of the dead, pictured as a hungry mouth.

The prophets did not object to music or wine. They objected to luxury that ignored God and the poor.
passages.later: Isaiah's contemporary Micah makes the same charge: ‘They covet fields and seize them; they take away houses’ (Micah 2:2). And the law said, ‘The land must not be sold permanently, because it is Mine’ (Leviticus 25:23).
passages.asks: The rich added field to field until they lived alone. Ask whether your own gains have pushed anyone out. And ask what the woe on those who ignore the work of God's hands says about how you spend your evenings.

passages.t: Woe to those who call evil good
passages.happening:
‘Woe to those who draw iniquity with cords of deceit and pull sin along with cart ropes’ (verse 18), who mock God and tell him to hurry up so they can see his plan (verse 19).

‘Woe to those who call evil good and good evil, who turn darkness to light and light to darkness, who replace bitter with sweet and sweet with bitter’ (verse 20). ‘Woe to those who are wise in their own eyes and clever in their own sight’ (verse 21). Woe to those who are heroes at drinking wine, ‘who acquit the guilty for a bribe and deprive the innocent of justice’ (verses 22-23).

As fire eats straw, their roots will rot and their blossoms blow away, for they rejected the LORD's instruction (verse 24). ‘Therefore the anger of the LORD burns against His people’ (verse 25). The mountains shake, and bodies lie in the streets. ‘Despite all this, His anger is not turned away; His hand is still upraised’ (verse 25).
passages.hearers:
The woes build. Sin is pulled along like a cart. The scoffers dare God to act. Moral language is turned upside down. The clever trust their own cleverness. Judges sell verdicts. These are not private failings. They are the sins of people with power and influence, and they corrupt a whole society.

The last woe joins drunkenness and bribery. The judges who should protect the innocent are heroes at the bottle and cowards at the bench.

Verse 25 has a refrain, that God's anger is not turned away and his hand is still raised. The same refrain returns in a series of poems in chapters 9 and 10. The first hearers would hear it as a drumbeat of warning: what has happened so far is not the end of it.
passages.later: Proverbs warns, ‘Be not wise in your own eyes; fear the LORD and turn away from evil’ (Proverbs 3:7). And Amos cries out against those ‘who turn justice into wormwood and cast righteousness to the ground’ (Amos 5:7).
passages.asks: Isaiah names people who call evil good and good evil. Ask where you have renamed something wrong so you would not have to stop. And ask whether you are wise in your own eyes about something God has spoken plainly on.

passages.t: God whistles for a distant army
passages.happening:
‘He lifts a banner for the distant nations and whistles for those at the ends of the earth’ (verse 26). They come swiftly. None grows weary or stumbles, no one sleeps, no belt is loose and no sandal strap broken (verse 27).

‘Their arrows are sharpened, and all their bows are strung. The hooves of their horses are like flint; their chariot wheels are like a whirlwind’ (verse 28). They roar like lions, seize their prey and carry it off, and no one can rescue it (verse 29).

In that day they will roar over the land like the sea. Whoever looks over the land will see darkness and distress, and even the light will be hidden by clouds (verse 30).
passages.hearers:
Isaiah does not name the army here, but chapters 7 and 10 identify God's instrument as Assyria, whose armies under Tiglath-pileser III (745 to 727 BC) and his successors were the most effective military force of the age. Assyrian palace reliefs show exactly what Isaiah describes: archers with drawn bows, chariots and cavalry.

The picture is frightening on purpose. God lifts a banner and whistles, as a man calls his dogs or his bees, and the greatest army in the world comes running. The first hearers were being told that the power they feared most was not outside God's control.

The chapter ends in darkness. The book does not stay there, but it does not skip it either.
passages.later: Isaiah later names the empire: ‘Woe to Assyria, the rod of My anger; the staff in their hands is My wrath’ (Isaiah 10:5). And he promises that God will judge Assyria too for its pride (Isaiah 10:12). Nahum later celebrates Assyria's fall: ‘For the wicked will never again march through you; they will be utterly cut off’ (Nahum 1:15).
passages.asks: The most feared army of the age comes when God whistles. Ask what power in your world you fear as if it were beyond God's reach. And ask how the darkness at the end of this chapter sits with you, before the light of the chapters that follow.
